changes.before: Create a view invitations with one name column combining names in morning and afternoon, with each distinct name once. Display it alphabetically. Preserve both source tables.
changes.after: Combine two name lists and remove repeated names.

before: UNION combines the rows produced by two SELECT queries.
Both queries must return the same number of columns. Here each returns a single name column.

UNION removes duplicate result rows.
```sql
SELECT 'Ari' AS name
UNION
SELECT 'Ari' AS name;
```
This returns one Ari row, not two.

UNION ALL keeps every result row, including repeated ones.
```sql
SELECT 'Ari' AS name
UNION ALL
SELECT 'Ari' AS name;
```
This returns two Ari rows. Keeping duplicates is useful when each occurrence represents a separate event.
Use UNION for one invitation per distinct name in this simplified exercise. In a real contact system, names alone are not reliable unique person identifiers.
ORDER BY at the end sorts the combined result. It does not decide which duplicates are removed.
A view can save the combined SELECT for reuse. The source rows remain in their original tables.
after: `UNION` combines the rows returned by SELECT queries.
Each query must return the same number of columns. Here, each returns one name.

Run this query:
```sql
SELECT 'Ari' AS name
UNION
SELECT 'Bo'
UNION
SELECT 'Ari'
ORDER BY name;
```
UNION removes repeated result rows.
The result is `Ari`, then `Bo`. Ari was supplied twice but is returned once.
`UNION ALL` keeps every result row, including repeats.
If this same query used UNION ALL, both Ari rows would stay. Keeping repeats is useful when each row means a separate event.
For this exercise, give one invitation to each distinct name. Real people can share a name, so a real contact system should use person IDs instead.
`ORDER BY` at the end sorts the combined result. It does not control duplicate removal.
Create `invitations(name)` as a view combining morning and afternoon with UNION. Display the view alphabetically and keep both source tables unchanged.
